notes.summary: Syllogism gives two or three statements, which you must accept as true even if they sound odd, and asks which conclusions definitely follow. SSC CGL uses the 'Only I / Only II / Either I or II / Neither / Both' format, sometimes with three conclusions or 'possibility' conclusions.
keyPoints: Draw Venn diagrams with only the overlap the statements force. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every possible diagram.
Conversions: All A are B → Some B are A; Some A are B → Some B are A; No A is B → No B is A; Some A are not B cannot be converted.
All + All = All (All A are B, All B are C → All A are C). All + No = No (All A are B, No B is C → No A is C).
Some + All = Some (Some A are B, All B are C → Some A are C). Some + No = Some-not (Some A are B, No B is C → Some A are not C).
Some + Some, All (A inside B) + Some (B with C), and No + No give no definite link between the two end terms.

Either-or: if neither conclusion follows by itself but the two form a complementary pair on the same terms (Some A are C / No A is C, or All A are C / Some A are not C), choose 'Either I or II' when that option is offered. If it is not offered, choose 'Neither'.
A possibility conclusion ('All X being Y is a possibility') follows if at least one valid diagram allows it and no statement rules it out.
Ignore real-world facts and judge only from the given statements.
traps: Converting 'All A are B' into 'All B are A'.
Treating a possible case as definite: 'Some roses are red' does not follow from 'All roses are flowers' and 'Some flowers are red'.
Marking 'Neither' when the two conclusions form a complementary pair and 'Either I or II' is one of the options.
Using real-world knowledge to accept or reject a conclusion.
notes.examTip: Draw the tightest diagram first, then try to draw one diagram that breaks each conclusion. If you can break it, that conclusion does not definitely follow.

questions.text:
Statements:
All roses are flowers.
Some flowers are red.
Conclusions:
I. Some roses are red.
II. Some flowers are roses.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
II: 'All roses are flowers' converts to 'Some flowers are roses', so II follows.
I: The red flowers may or may not include roses. A diagram with all roses outside the red part is possible, so I does not definitely follow.
So only II follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
No teacher is a doctor.
All doctors are singers.
Conclusions:
I. No doctor is a teacher.
II. Some singers are not teachers.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
I: 'No teacher is a doctor' converts directly to 'No doctor is a teacher', so I follows.
II: All doctors are singers, and none of them is a teacher, so at least the singers who are doctors are not teachers. II follows.
So both I and II follow.

questions.text:
Statements:
All pencils are erasers.
All erasers are sharpeners.
Conclusions:
I. All pencils are sharpeners.
II. All sharpeners are erasers.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
All + All gives All: pencils lie inside erasers, which lie inside sharpeners, so all pencils are sharpeners. I follows.
II reverses 'All erasers are sharpeners'. An 'All' statement cannot be reversed into another 'All' statement, so II does not follow.
So only I follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
All doctors are graduates.
Some graduates are writers.
Conclusions:
I. Some doctors are writers.
II. No doctor is a writer.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
The writers among the graduates may or may not include doctors, so neither I nor II is certain by itself.
But I (Some doctors are writers) and II (No doctor is a writer) are about the same two terms, and exactly one of them must be true.
This complementary pair gives 'Either I or II follows'.

questions.text:
Statements:
All cars are buses.
No bus is a truck.
Conclusions:
I. No car is a truck.
II. Some trucks being cars is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
All + No gives No: every car is a bus and no bus is a truck, so no car is a truck. I follows.
Because 'No car is a truck' is certain, any overlap between trucks and cars is impossible, so II does not follow.
So only I follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
Some fruits are vegetables.
No vegetable is a stone.
Conclusions:
I. Some fruits are not stones.
II. All stones being fruits is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
I: Some + No gives Some-not. The fruits that are vegetables cannot be stones, so some fruits are not stones. I follows.
II: Stones only have to stay away from vegetables. A diagram with all stones inside the part of fruits that is not vegetables breaks no statement, so the possibility holds and II follows.
So both I and II follow.

questions.text:
Statements:
All lions are tigers.
Some tigers are cats.
No cat is a dog.
Conclusions:
I. Some tigers are not dogs.
II. Some lions are cats.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
I: Some tigers are cats and no cat is a dog, so the tigers that are cats are not dogs (Some + No = Some-not). I follows.
II: The tigers that are cats may all lie outside the lion group, so 'Some lions are cats' is only possible, not certain. II does not follow.
So only I follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
Some players are not singers.
All singers are dancers.
Conclusions:
I. Some singers are not players.
II. Some dancers are singers.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
I: A 'Some A are not B' statement cannot be converted, so 'Some singers are not players' is not certain (all singers could be players). I does not follow.
II: 'All singers are dancers' converts to 'Some dancers are singers'. II follows.
So only II follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
No apple is a mango.
No mango is a banana.
Conclusions:
I. No apple is a banana.
II. Some bananas are apples.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
questions.explanation:
Two negative statements give no definite relation between apples and bananas, so neither I nor II follows by itself.
I (No apple is a banana) and II (Some bananas are apples, i.e. some apples are bananas) are a complementary pair on the same terms, so exactly one of them must be true.
So either I or II follows.

questions.text:
Statements:
All kites are planes.
Some planes are boats.
No boat is a car.
Conclusions:
I. Some planes are not cars.
II. All kites being boats is a possibility.
III. No kite is a car.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation:
I: Some planes are boats and no boat is a car, so those planes are not cars. I follows.
II: Kites lie inside planes, and nothing stops all of them from also lying in the plane-boat overlap, so the possibility holds. II follows.
III: Cars only have to avoid boats. Cars may overlap the part of the kites that is not boats, so 'No kite is a car' is not certain. III does not follow.
So only I and II follow.

questions.text:
Statements:
Some pens are pencils.
All pencils are rulers.
No ruler is a bag.
Conclusions:
I. Some pens are not bags.
II. No pencil is a bag.
III. Some rulers are pens.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements?
options: All I, II and III follow
questions.explanation:
II: All pencils are rulers and no ruler is a bag, so no pencil is a bag (All + No = No). II follows.
I: Some pens are pencils and no pencil is a bag, so those pens are not bags (Some + No = Some-not). I follows.
III: Some pens are pencils and all pencils are rulers, so some pens are rulers, which converts to 'Some rulers are pens'. III follows.
So all three conclusions follow.
